posts.title: Why we moved sensor logic to the edge
posts.author: priya-natarajan
posts.excerpt: Latency, resilience and a smaller attack surface: three reasons sensor logic now runs beside the PLC instead of in the cloud.
posts.description: Why Northwind moved sensor logic from the cloud to the edge beside the PLC: lower latency, resilience when the network drops and a smaller attack surface.
posts.body:
*[PLC]: programmable logic controller

Two years ago every sensor reading on a Northwind line went to the cloud before anything acted on it. That worked until it did not: a dairy in Norway lost its uplink for forty minutes and the line kept running, but the change log for those forty minutes was gone.

## Latency

A fill-level check that round-trips to a data centre takes two hundred milliseconds on a good day. A line that fills eighty bottles a minute does not have a good day every day. Running the check on the industrial PC beside the PLC takes under five milliseconds, every time.

## Resilience

Edge now buffers seventy-two hours of readings and changes locally. When the link comes back, the buffer syncs in order, and the change log has no gap. The dairy has had two more outages since; nobody noticed.

## A smaller attack surface

The PLC no longer needs a route to the internet at all. Edge talks to the PLC on one network port and to Cloud on the other, and nothing on the plant network can reach the controller through us.

## What changed for customers

Nothing visible, which was the point. Recipe limits still apply, the change log still exports in one click, and the reporting in Cloud looks the same. The difference shows up only when the network goes away.

posts.title: Letting line leads change recipes safely
posts.author: alex-morgan
posts.excerpt: Limits, logs and the two rules that make it work when the people on the floor adjust speeds and volumes themselves.
posts.description: How Northwind lets line leads change recipes without a programmer: engineer-set limits, an append-only change log and two rules that keep it safe.
posts.body:
*[PLC]: programmable logic controller
*[HMI]: human–machine interface

The most common support call we used to get was not a fault. It was a line lead asking for a fill volume to be changed by two millilitres, and an engineer being pulled off something else to type a number into a PLC.

## Rule one: engineers set the limits

Every value a line lead can change has a minimum, a maximum and a step, set by an engineer in the line description. Inside those limits, the line lead changes it from the HMI. Outside them, the change needs an engineer, and the screen says so.

## Rule two: everything is logged

Each change records who made it, when, from which screen, and what the old and new values were. The log is append-only and signed. Auditors like it more than the paper sheet it replaced.

## What we saw

Across the first hundred lines with recipe limits, engineer call-outs for recipe changes fell by nine in ten. Line leads made more changes, smaller ones, and reverted bad ones themselves because the log showed what they had changed.

## Where the limits come from

Usually from the first month of running: engineers look at the log, see which changes line leads keep making, and widen or narrow the limits. The description changes, the logic regenerates, and the HMI follows.

posts.title: How to read generated PLC code in an afternoon
posts.author: mei-chen
posts.excerpt: Four questions that get a reviewer through a generated program without reading every rung, and the one place to slow down.
posts.description: Four questions that get a reviewer through generated PLC code in an afternoon without reading every rung, and the one place where slowing down pays off.
posts.body:
Reviewers used to open a generated program the way they opened a hand-written one: at the top, rung by rung. It took days and found little, because the program is the description in another form. Here is the afternoon version.

## Does every interlock in the description appear in the code?

Studio lists them side by side. If the count matches and each one links to its rung, move on. If one is missing, stop; that is a description error, not a code error.

## Does any rung exist that no sentence produced?

Edited blocks are flagged in the audit trail. A flag means someone changed the code by hand; read that block fully.

## Do the recipe limits match the sheet the line lead signed?

Open the limits table next to the signed sheet. This is the one place to slow down, because a wrong maximum passes every test and fails on the floor.

## Do the acceptance tests cover each zone?

The test plan is generated per zone. An empty zone is a description with no rules in it, which is sometimes right and usually not.

Four questions, one afternoon, and a review that assessors accept because the evidence is on the page rather than in someone's memory.

---

> Describe the line, not the ladder. The ladder follows.
>
> — Priya Natarajan, *Control Engineering Review*

The review is **an afternoon, not a week**, because you read the *description* and let the tools read the code.

press.body:
Northwind Dynamics opened its third office today on King Fahd Road in Riyadh. The office provides Arabic-language support from 08:00 to 17:00 local time, Sunday to Thursday, and a delivery team for food and packaging plants across the Gulf.

"Plants in the region asked for support in their own hours and their own language," said Jonas Weber, Chief Executive. "Now they have both."

The Riyadh team starts with eight engineers led by Alex Morgan, Head of Delivery, and will grow to twenty by the end of 2027. Northwind now supports 1,284 lines in 19 countries from Manchester, Hamburg and Riyadh.

press.title: Thousandth Northwind line goes live
press.author: sofia-lindqvist
press.excerpt: A dairy in Norway becomes the thousandth production line running on generated, validated logic.
press.description: A filling line at a dairy in Norway is the thousandth production line to go live on Northwind, running on generated, validated PLC logic after nine days.
press.body:
A filling line at Fjord Dairy in Norway went live this week as the thousandth production line running on Northwind, nine days after the line was first described.

The line fills 80 bottles a minute and runs eleven recipes, all of which line leads adjust within limits set by the plant's engineers.

"Nine days from description to production is now the median, not the exception," said Priya Natarajan, Chief Technology Officer. "The thousandth line looked like the hundredth. That is the result we wanted."

Northwind lines run in food and beverage, pharmaceutical and automotive plants across 19 countries.

press.title: Northwind 4 released
press.author: sofia-lindqvist
press.excerpt: Generated logic for Beckhoff TwinCAT 3 joins Siemens and Rockwell, and the change log becomes append-only across every tier.
press.description: Northwind 4 adds generated logic for Beckhoff TwinCAT 3 alongside Siemens and Rockwell, and makes the recipe change log append-only in every tier.
press.body:
Northwind 4 is available today for all customers. The release adds a third controller family, Beckhoff TwinCAT 3, so one line description can now generate logic for Siemens, Rockwell and Beckhoff controllers.

The recipe change log is append-only in every tier from this release, with signed entries and checksummed exports.

"Customers asked for Beckhoff and for a log that auditors stop questioning," said Priya Natarajan, Chief Technology Officer. "Both are in 4."

Existing descriptions regenerate without changes. Studio, Edge and Cloud update in the maintenance window each plant chooses.

cases.title: Alder Foods cuts downtime by 38%
cases.quote: Our line leads fix most stops themselves now.
cases.excerpt: Four packing lines described in a month, and the stoppages that used to wait for an engineer now end at the HMI.
cases.description: How Alder Foods cut unplanned downtime by 38% on four packing lines by describing them in Northwind and letting line leads change recipes within limits.
cases.body:
*[HMI]: human–machine interface

Alder Foods runs four packing lines at one plant in the north of England. Before Northwind, every recipe change and most stoppages waited for one of two controls engineers.

## The problem

The lines stopped about twice a shift. Most stops were small: a wrong fill volume, a guard left open after cleaning, a changeover run in the wrong order. Each one waited for an engineer, and the engineers were usually on another line.

## What changed

The four lines were described in a month, one a week, by Alder's engineers with a Northwind engineer alongside. Recipe limits were set from the first month's change log. Line leads now adjust volumes and speeds at the HMI, and the HMI tells them why a stop happened.

## The result

Unplanned downtime fell by 38% in the first quarter. Engineer call-outs for recipe changes fell by nine in ten. The two engineers spend their time on the next plant.

The plant also avoids about 18 t of CO~2~ a year in commissioning trips, and gained 40 m^2^ of floor when the second control cabinet went.

cases.body:
Castor Automotive assembles sub-frames on a line of twelve robot cells and three conveyors in Germany.

## The problem

Safety reviews took a week and ended in arguments about hand-written safety logic that nobody could fully explain.

## What changed

The line was described zone by zone on a plant programme, one cell every three weeks. Safety logic was generated from the zone descriptions and reviewed sentence by sentence. The interlock walk-down was run with the HSE manager before the assessor arrived.

## The result

The safety review took two days and closed with no findings reopened. The plant has since described two more lines with its own engineers.

docs.title: Describe your first line
docs.summary: From a layout drawing to a generated program in an afternoon.
docs.description: A step-by-step guide to describing your first production line in Northwind Studio: stations, sensors, rules, recipes, and generating the first program.
docs.lede: From a layout drawing to a generated program in an afternoon.
docs.body:
*[HMI]: human–machine interface

## Before you start

You need Studio installed, a layout drawing or P&ID of the line, and the names your plant uses for its stations.

## Add the stations

Create one station per machine or process step, in line order. Give each the name on the drawing. A conveyor between two machines is its own station.

## Add sensors and actuators

For each station, list what it senses and what it moves. Use the template fields: name, type, controller address.

## Write the rules

Rules are sentences: "Start the filler only when the guard is closed and the conveyor is running." Interlocks are rules marked as safety rules; they cannot be changed from the HMI.

## Add recipes

A recipe is the set of values the line runs with for one product. For each value, set the minimum, maximum and step a line lead may use.

## Generate and review

Choose the controller family and generate. Studio shows each rung next to the sentence that produced it. Review, then run the generated acceptance tests.

### Shortcuts and output

Press [[Ctrl]]+[[G]] to generate, or [[Ctrl]]+[[Shift]]+[[R]] to open the review. With $n$ stations and $r$ rules, generation takes about $n$ + $r$ seconds. Station addresses use the plant's own notation, such as `DB10.DBX0.0`. A clean run ends like this:

```samp
Checked 6 stations, 14 rules, 2 interlocks
Generated 212 rungs in 11 s
No warnings
```

A rule written as text is kept verbatim in the description file:

```
rule "guard-open": when guard_1 is open, stop conveyor_1
```

docs.title: Connect a controller
docs.summary: Addresses, downloads and the first online check for Siemens, Rockwell and Beckhoff.
docs.description: How to connect Northwind Studio to a Siemens, Rockwell or Beckhoff controller: addresses, project download, the first online check and common errors.
docs.lede: Addresses, downloads and the first online check for each controller family.
docs.body:
## Choose the controller family

In the line description, set the controller family and model. Studio generates the project in that family's native format.

## Set the address

Enter the controller's IP address and, for Rockwell, the slot. Studio checks the connection before any download.

## Download the project

Download from Studio, or export the project and download with the vendor tool. Both paths produce the same code version in the change log.

## First online check

Go online and open the interlock list. Each interlock shows its live state next to its sentence. Walk the line and toggle each guard once.

## Common errors

- Connection refused: the controller is in a different subnet than Studio.
- Download rejected: the controller is in run mode with protection enabled.
- Interlock shows unknown: the sensor address does not match the drawing.

docs.title: Change a recipe
docs.summary: What a line lead can change at the HMI, what needs an engineer, and how the log records it.
docs.description: How line leads change recipe values at the HMI within engineer-set limits, what needs an engineer instead, and how every change is recorded in the log.
docs.lede: What a line lead can change at the HMI and how the log records it.
docs.body:
*[HMI]: human–machine interface

## At the HMI

Open the recipe screen, choose the product and change the value. The screen shows the minimum, maximum and step for that value. Save; the line applies the new value at the next cycle.

## Outside the limits

If the value you need is outside the limits, the screen says so and names the limit. An engineer widens the limit in the line description; the logic regenerates and the HMI follows.

## The change log

Every saved change records who, when, which screen, and the old and new values. Open the log from the recipe screen to see the history of the value you are looking at, or export the whole log from Cloud.

## Reverting a change

Open the log entry and choose revert. The revert is itself a logged change.

items.title: Which controllers are supported?
items.body: Siemens S7-1200 and S7-1500, Rockwell ControlLogix and CompactLogix, and Beckhoff TwinCAT 3.

items.title: Can we edit the generated code?
items.body: You can, but changes to the description are the supported path; edited blocks are flagged in the audit trail.

items.title: Where do descriptions live?
items.body: In your repository as text files; Studio reads and writes them like any editor.

items.title: How are updates applied?
items.body: Signed updates in a maintenance window you choose; the PLC keeps running throughout.

items.title: What does a rollout cost?
items.body: Starter is €490 (EUR) per line per month; a plant programme covers every line on a site for a site fee.

items.title: How long until the first line runs?
items.body: Most single lines are live within two weeks, including factory acceptance testing.

items.title: Can line operators change recipes?
items.body: Yes, within limits an engineer sets. Every change is logged with who, when and what.

items.title: Where is our data stored?
items.body: In the EU by default, on premise with the Enterprise tier.

faqPricing.title: Is there a minimum term?
faqPricing.body: No. Starter and Plant are monthly and you can cancel any month.

faqPricing.title: What counts as a line?
faqPricing.body: One description running on one or more PLCs that move product from one end to the other.

faqPricing.title: Do prices include support?
faqPricing.body: Yes. Email support in Starter, phone support within four hours in Plant, a named engineer in Enterprise.

faqPricing.title: Can we switch tiers?
faqPricing.body: Any month, in either direction. Descriptions and logs carry over.

faqTrust.title: Where is data hosted?
faqTrust.body: In the EU, in two regions; Enterprise customers can host on premise.

faqTrust.title: How do you handle a vulnerability report?
faqTrust.body: We acknowledge within two working days and publish a fix note when the fix ships.

faqTrust.title: Who can access customer data?
faqTrust.body: Support engineers only with time-limited access you grant, and every access is logged.

faqTrust.title: Do you have a security questionnaire ready?
faqTrust.body: Yes. Ask the security contact below and we send the current one the same day.

glossary.definition: The plain-language model of a line that Northwind generates logic from.
A condition that must hold before an action is allowed, such as a guard being closed before a motor starts.
The set of values a line runs with for one product: speeds, volumes, temperatures.
The minimum, maximum and step an engineer allows a line lead to use for one recipe value.
The append-only record of who changed which value, when, from where, and what it was before.
One machine or process step in a line description, with its sensors, actuators and rules.
A test generated from the description and run before a line goes into production.
The exported set of tests, results, code versions and sign-offs an assessor reviews.
